tables_dir <- file.path(project_root, "output", "tables")
figures_dir <- file.path(project_root, "output", "figures")
processed_dir <- file.path(project_root, "data", "processed")
table_path <- function(name) file.path(tables_dir, name)
figure_path <- function(name) file.path(figures_dir, name)
format_count <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)

# A missing artefact is evidence that its analysis has not completed.  The
# report marks it as such rather than substituting an invented result.
read_table_if_available <- function(name) {
  path <- table_path(name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) return(NULL)
  utils::read.csv(path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)
}
show_table_or_notice <- function(data, caption, digits = 3) {
  if (is.null(data)) {
    cat("*This result is not available yet. Render after its analysis script has completed.*\n\n")
  } else {
    print(knitr::kable(data, digits = digits, caption = caption))
  }
}
include_figure_if_available <- function(name, caption = NULL) {
  path <- figure_path(name)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    cat("*Not yet available: `", name, "`.*\n\n", sep = "")
    return(invisible(FALSE))
  }
  if (!is.null(caption)) cat("*", caption, "*\n\n", sep = "")
  # Emit Markdown directly so the path is resolved from the project root even
  # when knitr's input-directory and root-directory conventions differ.
  image_path <- normalizePath(path, winslash = "/", mustWork = TRUE)
  cat(sprintf("![%s](%s)\n\n", name, image_path))
  invisible(TRUE)
}
emit_code_file <- function(path, language) {
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    cat("*Source file unavailable: `", path, "`.*\n\n", sep = "")
    return(invisible(FALSE))
  }
  cat("```", language, "\n", sep = "")
  cat(paste(readLines(path, warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n"))
  cat("\n```\n\n")
  invisible(TRUE)
}

# Abstract

This report documents a fully Bayesian analysis plan for US residential listing
prices using the USA Real Estate Dataset. The outcome is log listing price and
the intended hierarchy represents broad state differences together with local
state--ZIP variation. The model sequence compares a pooled regression (M0), a
state random-intercept model (M1), and a state--ZIP random-intercept model
(M2), using MCMC to approximate posterior and predictive distributions.

The completed audit records `r format_count(overview_value("rows"))` raw
listings and establishes the modelling data contract: positive price and house
size, log-scale response and living area, `log1p` lot size, categorical listing
status, and state--ZIP labels. The core completed result is the reproducible
data audit and frozen analysis design. Production posterior draws and their
derived results are deliberately marked unavailable until the corresponding
scripts have run; this avoids presenting missing computation as Bayesian
evidence.

# Introduction

## Motivation

Two properties with similar observed features can have different listing prices
because their geographic contexts differ. State conditions may shift the broad
housing market, while smaller local differences can remain within a state. A
model that ignores this structure risks assigning unobserved geographic
variation to property characteristics or reporting unstable local estimates.

The analysis models both the listings and the unknown quantities that govern
their distribution. This makes uncertainty part of the analysis: prior
distributions represent pre-data uncertainty, the likelihood represents the
conditional data model, and the posterior results from conditioning on the
observed listings.

## Research questions

1. After adjusting for measured property features and listing status, how much
   descriptive log-price variation is associated with states and state--ZIP
   groups?
2. Does adding state and ZIP hierarchy improve predictive performance relative
   to the same pooled covariate model?
3. Can the fitted hierarchy reproduce relevant log-price and geographic
   features in replicated data?

The geographic effects are descriptive and predictive associations, not causal
effects. Property condition, school quality, amenities, listing strategy, and
other relevant determinants are not observed here.

# Data and preprocessing

## Source and raw-data evidence

The source is the [USA Real Estate Dataset](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ahmedshahriarsakib/usa-real-estate-dataset),
version 25, downloaded on 21 June 2026 and preserved unchanged as
`data/raw/realtor-data.csv`. Its recorded MD5 checksum is
`09ce5bd36ef648a5769a996735c05951`.

The audit describes the source before filters are applied. This distinction is
statistically important: a cleaning rule changes the population represented by
the likelihood, so its consequences should be visible before a model is fit.

```{r raw-overview, results='asis'}
# Theory note: ZIP digits are labels used to define groups; treating them as a
# continuous predictor would impose a numerical ordering with no meaning.
show_table_or_notice(overview, "Raw dataset coverage before modelling filters.")
show_table_or_notice(dictionary, "Data dictionary and completeness before modelling filters.")
```

## Missingness, valid values, and transformations

The planned complete-case model needs price, house size, lot size, bedrooms,
bathrooms, status, state, and ZIP label. Missingness is a modelling decision,
not cosmetic cleanup. Positive price and house size are required because their
logarithms are used. Zero acreage remains valid: `log1p(acre_lot)` maps it to
zero while reducing leverage from exceptionally large lots.

```{r raw-quality-tables, results='asis'}
# Theory note: logging positive, right-skewed quantities can make a Gaussian
# residual model more plausible; it is not a rule for deleting expensive homes.
if (!is.null(missingness)) {
  missingness_display <- missingness
  missingness_display$missing_percent <- 100 * missingness_display$missing_prop
  missingness_display <- missingness_display[c("variable", "missing_n", "missing_percent")]
  print(knitr::kable(
    missingness_display, digits = 2,
    col.names = c("Variable", "Missing listings", "Missing (%)"),
    caption = "Missingness in unfiltered raw listings."
  ))
} else {
  show_table_or_notice(NULL, "Missingness in unfiltered raw listings.")
}
show_table_or_notice(quality_counts, "Value-quality checks before modelling filters.")
show_table_or_notice(status_counts, "Listing-status distribution before modelling filters.")
```

## Sampling and analysis frame

ZIP is represented as a state--ZIP label: a local effect belongs to the state
in which that ZIP appears. The frozen design samples listings within selected
ZIP groups and divides each group into training and held-out rows. The held-out
exercise evaluates a new listing in a known ZIP; prediction for a genuinely new
ZIP is a separate posterior simulation.

```{r data-decisions-and-sample, results='asis'}
# Theory note: scaling is learned from training rows only, keeping held-out
# outcomes outside the fitted likelihood and the prior-relevant scale.
show_table_or_notice(decisions, "Pre-specified modelling decisions supported by the audit.")
show_table_or_notice(row_accounting, "Row accounting through the modelling frame.")
show_table_or_notice(sample_overview, "Frozen analysis-sample dimensions.")
if (!is.null(sample_manifest)) {
  manifest_summary <- stats::aggregate(n ~ split, data = sample_manifest, FUN = sum)
  print(knitr::kable(
    manifest_summary, col.names = c("Split", "Listings"),
    caption = "Listings represented by the saved state--ZIP sampling manifest."
  ))
} else {
  cat("*The sampling manifest is not available yet.*\n\n")
}
```

The stratified sample preserves the selected hierarchy while making MCMC
diagnostics, recovery experiments, and replicated-data checks feasible. It is
not a design for a population-weighted national mean listing price.

# Bayesian models and priors

## Joint model and targets

Let `y` denote the observed listings and let `\theta` collect regression
coefficients, residual scale, and geographic effects. The Bayesian model is one
joint distribution,

$$
p(y, \theta) = p(y \mid \theta)\pi(\theta),
$$

where `p(y \mid \theta)` is the conditional data model and `\pi(\theta)` is the
prior distribution. Once `y` is observed, coherent conditioning yields

$$
p(\theta \mid y) =
\frac{p(y \mid \theta)\pi(\theta)}{m(y)}, \qquad
m(y) = \int p(y \mid \theta)\pi(\theta)\,d\theta.
$$

The denominator both normalises the posterior and defines the prior predictive
density. Posterior summaries describe uncertain parameters; predictive
distributions additionally include variation in a future listing.

## Model sequence and partial pooling

For listing `i`, define standardized log price `y_i`, covariate vector
`\boldsymbol{x}_i`, state `s[i]`, and ZIP group `z[i]`. M0--M2 use identical
response, covariates, training rows, and priors; only geographic structure
changes:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{M0:}\quad &y_i \sim \operatorname{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma),
&& \mu_i = \alpha + \boldsymbol{x}_i^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol{\beta},\\
\text{M1:}\quad &y_i \sim \operatorname{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma),
&& \mu_i = \alpha + \boldsymbol{x}_i^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol{\beta} + u_{s[i]},\\
\text{M2:}\quad &y_i \sim \operatorname{Normal}(\mu_i, \sigma),
&& \mu_i = \alpha + \boldsymbol{x}_i^\mathsf{T}\boldsymbol{\beta}
+ u_{s[i]} + v_{z[i]}.
\end{aligned}
$$

In M2,

$$
u_s \sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, \mathit{sd}_{\mathrm{state}}), \qquad
v_z \sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, \mathit{sd}_{\mathrm{ZIP}}).
$$

Partial pooling follows from these group distributions. A ZIP with little
information is estimated less precisely and pulled more toward its population
mean, while a well-observed ZIP can depart when the data support it. This
regularises local estimates probabilistically; it does not establish that a
location causes a price difference.

```{r hierarchical-dag, echo=FALSE, fig.cap='Directed acyclic graph for the planned M2 hierarchy. Arrows encode conditional dependence, not causal effects.', fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
# Theory note: the graph exposes the factorisation. Hyperpriors govern the
# distributions of state and ZIP effects; those effects help determine log price.
graphics::par(mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
graphics::plot.new()
graphics::plot.window(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 6))
draw_node <- function(x, y, label, fill) {

}

}
draw_node(1.2, 5.0, "priors for\nalpha, beta, sigma", "#D9EDF7")
```

## Priors and prior-predictive evidence

The response and continuous covariates are standardized from training rows.
The intercept prior is centred at zero, coefficients have weakly informative
Normal priors, and scales have proper half-Normal priors. Proper priors provide
a defined posterior while retaining room for the likelihood to update beliefs.

Prior-predictive simulation draws parameters from their priors and then draws
outcomes from the likelihood. It tests whether the full model can generate
plausible listings before the observed response is used.

```{r prior-predictive-results, results='asis'}
# Theory note: prior prediction averages over uncertain parameters; it is more
# informative than checking a prior on each coefficient in isolation.
show_table_or_notice(prior_settings, "Prior-predictive simulation settings.")
show_table_or_notice(prior_ranges, "Prior-predictive price-range summary.")
include_figure_if_available(
  "prior_predictive_price_ranges.png",
  "Prior-predictive ranges after simulated log prices are converted to dollars."
)
```

# Simulation study

The recovery study generates synthetic outcomes from known M2 parameter values,
fits the same workflow, and compares posterior intervals with the generating
truth. This is an implementation check rather than proof that the real-data
model is true. Repeated simulations can assess interval coverage and typical
error rather than relying on a single favourable result.

```{r simulation-recovery-results, results='asis'}
# Theory note: simulation makes the unknown parameter observable by construction,
# so calibration of a posterior interval can be evaluated directly.
show_table_or_notice(
  read_table_if_available("simulation_recovery_settings.csv"),
  "Simulation-recovery MCMC settings."
)
show_table_or_notice(
  read_table_if_available("simulation_recovery_full_scalar_parameters.csv"),
  "Recovery of scalar parameters from a synthetic M2 dataset."
)
show_table_or_notice(
  read_table_if_available("simulation_recovery_repeated_parameter_metrics.csv"),
  "Repeated-simulation recovery metrics."
)
include_figure_if_available(
  "simulation_recovery_scalar_parameters.png",
  "Posterior intervals and known scalar parameters in the recovery study."
)
```

# MCMC computation and diagnostics

The hierarchical posterior is not expected to have a convenient analytic form.
MCMC produces dependent draws whose long-run distribution is the posterior.
For a posterior summary `h(\theta)`, the simulation estimate is

$$
\widehat{I}_T = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}h\left(\theta^{(t)}\right).
$$

Successive draws can be autocorrelated, so the number of iterations alone is
not an accuracy measure. Positive autocorrelation lowers effective sample size
and increases Monte Carlo error. Multiple chains with dispersed initial values,
trace plots, running means, autocorrelation plots, split R-hat, bulk/tail ESS,
and MCSE assess complementary features of the numerical approximation.

```{r mcmc-diagnostics-results, results='asis'}
# Theory note: diagnostics concern the MCMC approximation conditional on the
# model. They cannot by themselves establish that the model is adequate.
show_table_or_notice(
  read_table_if_available("m2_selected_diagnostics.csv"),
  "Selected M2 convergence and Monte Carlo accuracy diagnostics."
)
include_figure_if_available("m2_trace_plots.png", "Trace plots for pre-specified M2 parameters.")
include_figure_if_available("m2_autocorrelation_plots.png", "Autocorrelation plots for pre-specified M2 parameters.")
```

Posterior claims should be made only after all pre-specified visual and numeric
criteria are satisfied. A failure prompts investigation of code, priors,
indexing, initial values, adaptation, or chain length rather than selective use
of appealing summaries.

# Posterior results

Posterior summaries report medians or means, 95% credible intervals, and
posterior probability statements. A 95% credible interval has 0.95 posterior
probability under the stated model and prior. Fixed-effect estimates are
conditional associations on standardized log price; state and ZIP effects are
residual geographic associations after the measured covariates are included.

For a future outcome `y^{\mathrm{new}}`, the target is the posterior predictive
distribution,

$$
p(y^{\mathrm{new}} \mid y) =
\int p(y^{\mathrm{new}} \mid \theta)p(\theta \mid y)\,d\theta.
$$

It includes both parameter uncertainty and irreducible listing variation, so a
predictive interval is generally wider than an interval for a conditional mean.

```{r posterior-results, results='asis'}
# Theory note: shrinkage must be read with sample size and interval width, not
# ranked as causal evidence about one location versus another.
show_table_or_notice(
  read_table_if_available("m2_fixed_effects.csv"),
  "M2 fixed-effect posterior summaries on the standardized log-price scale."
)
show_table_or_notice(
  read_table_if_available("m2_hierarchical_variance_summary.csv"),
  "M2 residual, state, and ZIP variation summaries."
)
show_table_or_notice(
  read_table_if_available("m2_posterior_predictions.csv"),
  "M2 posterior-predictive scenarios on the dollar scale."
)
include_figure_if_available("m2_state_effects_caterpillar.png", "M2 state effects with credible intervals.")
include_figure_if_available("m2_selected_zip_effects_caterpillar.png", "Selected M2 ZIP effects with credible intervals.")
include_figure_if_available("m2_posterior_prediction_intervals.png", "Posterior-predictive intervals for selected scenarios.")
```

# Model comparison and checking

## Comparative predictive evidence

Deviance Information Criterion (DIC) is a complexity-adjusted, in-sample
comparison. With `D(\theta) = -2\log L(\theta)`, it combines fit with an
effective parameter count. It is comparable only when the models use the same
observations and likelihood convention, and it has no useful absolute scale.

Held-out evaluation uses the same test rows for M0, M1, and M2. RMSE and MAE
measure predictive error, interval coverage checks calibration, and mean log
predictive density rewards well-calibrated sharp distributions. These evaluate
different properties, so no single criterion chooses a model by itself.

```{r comparison-results, results='asis'}
# Theory note: lower DIC does not prove model adequacy; held-out predictions and
# replicated-data checks test aspects that an in-sample criterion cannot see.
show_table_or_notice(
  read_table_if_available("dic_comparison.csv"),
  "DIC decomposition for comparable fitted models."
)
show_table_or_notice(
  read_table_if_available("heldout_predictive_metrics.csv"),
  "Held-out predictive performance using common test listings."
)
```

## Posterior-predictive checks

Posterior-predictive checking generates replicated datasets from the fitted
model and compares them with the observed training data. Relevant discrepancies
include the log-price distribution, upper tails, and state or ZIP variation. A
mismatch diagnoses a feature to improve; it is not a mechanical pass/fail test.

```{r posterior-predictive-results, results='asis'}
# Theory note: replicated outcomes include residual variation, whereas fitted
# means alone can conceal a model's failure to reproduce observed dispersion.
show_table_or_notice(
  read_table_if_available("posterior_predictive_check_summary.csv"),
  "Observed-versus-replicated posterior-predictive discrepancy summaries."
)
include_figure_if_available(
  "posterior_predictive_checks_m2.png",
  "Observed and replicated M2 distributional and geographic features."
)
```

# Discussion

The completed work provides a transparent empirical foundation: the raw source
is preserved, data quality is measured before filtering, transformations are
explicit, and the state--ZIP sample is reproducible. The questions above can be
answered substantively only when recovery, converged posterior draws,
held-out evaluation, and posterior-predictive artefacts are available.

The data are online listings rather than a random sample of completed sales.
They omit reliable measures of property condition, school quality,
neighbourhood amenities, and a usable time axis; repeated listings may remain
even where exact duplicate rows do not. These limitations preclude causal
interpretation, and the balanced computational sample does not justify a
population-weighted national conclusion.

```{r report-artifact-status}
# Theory note: a reproducible report makes the boundary between completed
# evidence and planned analysis visible to readers and future re-renders.
knitr::kable(
  artifact_status[, c("report_section", "status")],
  col.names = c("Report section", "Current artifact status"),
  caption = "Availability of evidence displayed by this render."
)
```

## JAGS model code

The following source files specify the likelihood and priors. JAGS uses
precision in its Normal distribution, so the code converts each positive
standard deviation to inverse variance. Including executable source makes the
probability model inspectable rather than merely described in prose.

### M0: pooled regression

```{r appendix-m0, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
emit_code_file(file.path(project_root, "models", "m0_pooled.jags"), "jags")
```

### M1: state random intercepts

```{r appendix-m1, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}

```

### M2: nested state and ZIP random intercepts
